startup.name: flowscope
startup.one_liner: AI implementation firm that maps and automates business processes
startup.description: flowscope is an AI implementation firm that deploys agents to map, optimize, and automate companies’ processes end to end

yc_acceptance.basis: Test note: this company was accepted to YC, so this is only the forward estimate. Starting prior is about 1 percent for a random applicant (0.6 to 2 percent third party range, per references/yc_acceptance.md). Factors from the table: no stated technical founder or revenue (neutral), two founders (neutral), a services-like idea in a crowded 2026 'AI implementation' category (down), but it fits the YC pattern of agents applied to boring operations (small up). Net about 1.2 percent, inside the 0.3 to 15 percent guard rail.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most likely say the pitch sounds like a consulting firm with an AI label: two founders, no named customers, no sign that the agent product is better than what Lume, Sero or Onboard.io tried, and a crowded field of implementation and workflow vendors. Without proof of paid pilots, partners may see low software margins and a hard to scale services motion.

anchors.adjustment_reason: Seed is 0.94x the B2B 2022-25 anchor of 59 percent: a young AI wave and 2026 appetite for agent companies offset the services-like risk. Within the 0.75x guard rail.

bands.rationale: Small pre-seed of about 600K to 1.5M on a SAFE, barely above the YC deal. Services revenue may fund it without a priced round.
Typical 2026 seed near the 3.0M US median deal size and 18M pre money from PitchBook NVCA via Equidam (see stage_benchmarks.md). Paid pilots with mid sized companies convert into a lead investor.
Strong seed led by a known fund, near the YC 2022+ announced median of 4.1M or above. A fast growing forward deployed agent story attracts a hot seed.
Upside seed or large first round if usage or revenue spikes, common for hot AI categories in 2026. A pivot into a vertical product can reset the multiple.

ladder.why_it_fails: Flowscope is two people selling process mapping and automation to companies. The seed step above the standard 500K deal fails if early revenue is project based and investors price it as a consultancy, as happened to services-like implementation startups such as Sero, which shows no funding found after its batch. Another miss is that no pilot customer renews, so there is no repeatable story to fund.

Flowscope would fail if each deployment needs bespoke work by the two founders, as Lume stayed at five people and was acquired for talent rather than raising a Series A. Competitors with product led onboarding agents and large integrators can undercut price.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series B needs a repeatable platform with sales hires and net retention. This step fails if deployments never turn into a product, the team stays small, and customers treat the agents as a project. Onboard.io stayed a small SaaS and sold in 2025 without a B, which is the usual outcome for this path.

bands.rationale: Modest C or growth round, or venture debt plus equity. Late rounds are rare for companies with this start.
Typical C or later; 2022+ YC median C is 45M, D plus 97.5M. Needs profitable growth.
Breakout later round at multi billion value. Needs category leadership.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series C or later requires a category leading platform. It fails here because implementation work is service heavy, large systems integrators and model labs sell similar forward deployed agents, and few companies in this class reach scale. Auctor from 2025 shows the upside, but needs a clear enterprise wedge first.

outcomes.why_it_fails: Most likely failure is that the company stays a small agency style firm, never builds a product that investors value on a software multiple, and stalls or is acquired for talent. Lume and Sero show that implementation startups in this wave stayed small. A pivot into a vertical product is the way out, but is not the base case.

killers.evidence: Process mapping done end to end for each customer is labor heavy and investors price it as consulting.
killers.mitigation: Productize the mapping step and charge recurring platform fees.

killers.evidence: Rocketlane, ServiceNow and automation vendors plus forward deployed AI shops serve the same buyers.
killers.mitigation: Pick one industry and process and show faster time to value.

killers.evidence: Every deployment needs founder time, which caps growth in the first year.
killers.mitigation: Hire a deployment engineer early and standardize templates.

technical_complexity.rationale: Agents that map and automate processes across varied company systems need integrations, reliability and evaluation. A two person team can build a demo in three months, but making deployments robust across customers is the hard part, and the models are rented.

who: Foundation model labs with agent products
takeover_risk.rationale: Incumbents and labs already ship workflow agents and have distribution, so a copy of the core idea needs only months. The remaining moat is customer specific process knowledge.

Onboarding and implementation software is an established funded category.

brand.rationale: The name suggests visibility into flows, which fits the mapping pitch. Past YC names in this class such as Lume and Sero are short and neutral too. The name neither helps nor hurts, and the invented or proper name class shows no outcome edge in the name data.

narrative.headline: A two person AI implementation firm with a believable need but a services trap; seed is likely, later rounds depend on turning into a product.
narrative.general_summary: Flowscope sells agents that map and automate business processes end to end. Demand for automation is real and 2026 investor appetite for agent companies is high, so a seed above the standard deal is more likely than not. The weakness is the shape of the business: it reads as an implementation firm, which usually means project revenue, low margin and founder bound delivery. YC analogs such as Lume and Sero stayed small and sold for talent or showed no later rounds. The ladder therefore sits near the B2B cohort anchors with a mild discount at Series A and a wide band at later stages.
